subject: Edge finishing and assembly quality
hook: Why the door edge is thicker than the shelf back.
ig:
Why the door edge is thicker than the shelf back: it's about where the knocks land.

Look at a kitchen after a few years of family life. The damage is almost always in the same places: the bottom edge of base doors, drawer fronts by the bin and the corner of a tall unit by the doorway.

Those are the edges that need 2 mm ABS. It has more body to take a knock without chipping through to the board.

Now look at the back edge of a shelf, or a carcass edge pressed against a wall. Nobody will ever touch it. That's where 0.4 mm does the job perfectly well.

Specifying thickness edge by edge, rather than one thickness for everything, puts the strength where it's needed.

Working on a cutting list now? Tell us in the comments which edge you find gets the most wear on your jobs. Our edge banding service is via the link in bio.
fb:
A small detail that makes a big difference to how furniture wears: not every edge needs the same edging.

Door and drawer fronts take knocks every day, so they suit a thicker 2 mm ABS edge. The back of a shelf or a carcass edge against a wall never gets touched, so 0.4 mm is plenty there.

Getting this right on a cutting list puts the strength where it counts.
